# People around Agastya

3223 person-like nodes in 4199 passage claims. A direct claim names a source-local Agastya facet as an endpoint. Context claims connect other figures in the same source tradition. Neither kind proves a historical meeting.

Claim status is a review level: `translation_checked` concerns a translated text, `source_text_checked` concerns the Sanskrit text, `editorial_attribution` marks assigned speakers or authors, `scholarly_report` is second-hand, and `identity_hypothesis` is a proposed identification.

## Abhaya · Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son in the CE birth-order roster

Type: person. Direct links: 0. Context links: 1.

### Context in the same passages

- **MBAR117** Abhaya · Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son in the CE birth-order roster → son of → Dhṛtarāṣṭra · Viṣṇu Purāṇa 4.20 witness. [Mahābhārata, Ādiparvan, BORI Critical Edition electronic text, Mahābhārata Ādiparvan 1.108.12](https://bombay.indology.info/mahabharata/text/UR/MBh01.txt). translation_checked. Abhaya is named in the sequence of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s sons. The CE asks for Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s sons by name and says the roster follows their birth order (1.108.1, 15). Paired dual forms and the triple Dṛḍharatha are represented as distinct people by Sanskrit number; repeated exact names are handled as unresolved references.

[Mahābhārata, Vana Parva, Ganguli §99, Vana Parva, Ganguli §99](https://sacred-texts.com/hin/m03/m03099.htm). translation_checked. Lomasa says the foetus remained in Lopāmudrā’s womb seven years before Dṛḍhasyu was born; as a child he carried sacrificial fuel and was called Idhmavāha. The epithet and the seven-year gestation belong to this epic story; they do not independently date Agastya or identify a different Dṛḍhasyu.
- **EEX018** Agastya’s ancestors / Pitṛs → are released after birth of → Dṛḍhasyu / Idhmavāha · epic witness. [Mahābhārata, Vana Parva, Ganguli §99, Vana Parva, Ganguli §99](https://sacred-texts.com/hin/m03/m03099.htm). translation_checked. The narration says Agastya’s ancestors obtain the desired state after he begets Dṛḍhasyu. This is the story’s stated consequence of the son’s birth.

### Review notes

- Vana Parva §99: Dṛḍhasyu is born after seven years in the womb and is also called Idhmavāha for carrying fuel.

### Questions

- Keep separate from other figures with the same or similar name unless independently identified.

Agastya is only the intended object of Kānthan’s visit in this episode; the passage does not narrate their encounter. Paraśurāma is a named person in Kānthan’s reported expectation, not a participant in the scene.

This claim records the prediction and outcome, not an identity for the son.

[Mahābhārata, Vana Parva, Ganguli §97, Vana Parva, Ganguli §97](https://sacred-texts.com/hin/m03/m03097.htm). translation_checked. Seeing her parents distressed, Lopāmudrā tells her father to give her to Agastya and spare himself anxiety. The daughter’s own consent is explicit in this telling.
- **EEX010** Lopāmudrā → practices austerities with → Agastya · Mahābhārata. [Mahābhārata, Vana Parva, Ganguli §97, Vana Parva, Ganguli §97](https://sacred-texts.com/hin/m03/m03097.htm). translation_checked. After their marriage, Agastya and Lopāmudrā go to Gaṅgādvāra and practice austerities together. Narrated after the marriage; this is a narrative sequence, with no absolute date.
- **EEX011** Lopāmudrā → requests wealth and royal attire from → Agastya · Mahābhārata. [Mahābhārata, Vana Parva, Ganguli §97, Vana Parva, Ganguli §97](https://sacred-texts.com/hin/m03/m03097.htm). translation_checked. Before agreeing to marital intercourse, Lopāmudrā asks Agastya for a bed, adornments and attire like those she had in her father’s palace. This request motivates Agastya’s subsequent search for wealth; no modern chronological inference is implied.
- **REX006** Agastya · Buddhacarita reception → story also names → Lopāmudrā. [Buddhacarita 4.73: Sanskrit and Cowell translation, 4.73](https://www.wisdomlib.org/buddhism/book/the-buddha-carita-sanskrit/d/doc345043.html). translation_checked. The same verse also names Lopāmudrā. Cowell’s English for the second half of 4.73 is difficult; this records co-mention only, without inferring kinship or a second event.
- **REX008** Lopāmudrā → is assigned speech in → Agastya · Vedic witnesses. [Bṛhaddevatā 4.55–64, Agastya and Lopāmudrā, 4.58; RV 1.179.1–2](https://www.wisdomlib.org/hinduism/book/brihaddevata-attributed-to-shaunaka/d/doc1621782.html). editorial_attribution. Lopāmudrā is assigned the first two verses.
- **REX009** Agastya · Vedic witnesses → is assigned reply to → Lopāmudrā. [Bṛhaddevatā 4.55–64, Agastya and Lopāmudrā, 4.58; RV 1.179.3–4](https://www.wisdomlib.org/hinduism/book/brihaddevata-attributed-to-shaunaka/d/doc1621782.html). editorial_attribution. Agastya is assigned the next two verses.

### Context in the same passages

- **EEX017** Dṛḍhasyu / Idhmavāha · epic witness → is born after seven years in womb of → Lopāmudrā. [Mahābhārata, Vana Parva, Ganguli §99, Vana Parva, Ganguli §99](https://sacred-texts.com/hin/m03/m03099.htm). translation_checked. Lomasa says the foetus remained in Lopāmudrā’s womb seven years before Dṛḍhasyu was born; as a child he carried sacrificial fuel and was called Idhmavāha. The epithet and the seven-year gestation belong to this epic story; they do not independently date Agastya or identify a different Dṛḍhasyu.

### Review notes

- RV 1.179 is already covered in the graph as a marital dialogue with Agastya.

### Questions

- The speaker labels are editorial/traditional; no additional independent Vedic passage connecting her to Agastya was verified in this collection.
- A possible Lopāmudrā interpretation of RV 1.170.4’s dual verb is discussed by Jamison–Brereton, p. 370; left unclaimed because the text does not name her there.

<a id="maruts"></a>
## Maruts

Type: deity_collective. Direct links: 4. Context links: 1.

### Direct Agastya links

- **C004** Agastya · Vedic witnesses → mentions → Maruts. [Ṛgveda 1.170, 1.170.2, 5](https://sacred-texts.com/hin/rigveda/rv01170.htm). translation_checked. The appeal concerns the Maruts.
- **VEX001** Agastya · Vedic witnesses → appeals to → Maruts. [The Rigveda: The Earliest Religious Poetry of India, Ṛgveda 1.171.1–4](https://wiswo.org/books/_resources/book-reference-pdfs/Jamison-Brereton-2014-The%20Rigveda-The%20Earliest%20Poetry%20of%20India%20all%203%20Volume%20Sets.pdf). editorial_attribution. The hymn voice asks the Maruts to set aside their anger and forgive the speaker after Soma intended for them was given away. Speaker divisions are an editorial reconstruction; the hymn itself does not identify each speech by speaker name.
- **VEX006** Agastya · Vedic witnesses → appeases → Maruts. [The Rigveda: The Earliest Religious Poetry of India, Ṛgveda 1.165, speaker divisions and introduction, pp. 360–361](https://wiswo.org/books/_resources/book-reference-pdfs/Jamison-Brereton-2014-The%20Rigveda-The%20Earliest%20Poetry%20of%20India%20all%203%20Volume%20Sets.pdf). editorial_attribution. In the editorial division of 1.165, the closing verses assigned to Agastya address the Maruts and offer them his hymn. Jamison–Brereton assign 1.165.13–15 to Agastya; the dialogue structure and individual speakers are editorially analyzed.
- **VEX007** Agastya · Vedic witnesses → is attributed a hymn to → Maruts. [The Rigveda: The Earliest Religious Poetry of India, Ṛgveda 1.172 introduction, p. 371](https://wiswo.org/books/_resources/book-reference-pdfs/Jamison-Brereton-2014-The%20Rigveda-The%20Earliest%20Poetry%20of%20India%20all%203%20Volume%20Sets.pdf). scholarly_report. The three-verse Marut hymn 1.172 is identified in the edition as a short pendant to Agastya’s Indra–Marut hymn cycle. Traditional/editorial hymn attribution does not establish personal authorship or a historical encounter.

### Context in the same passages

- **VEX003** Indra → is called brother of → Maruts. [The Rigveda: The Earliest Religious Poetry of India, Ṛgveda 1.170.2; Jamison–Brereton translation, p. 370](https://wiswo.org/books/_resources/book-reference-pdfs/Jamison-Brereton-2014-The%20Rigveda-The%20Earliest%20Poetry%20of%20India%20all%203%20Volume%20Sets.pdf). translation_checked. Agastya says to Indra that the Maruts are Indra’s brothers. This wording is in 1.170.2, not 1.171.2; attribution of the speech is based on editorial verse divisions.

### Review notes

- RV 1.171 has the attributed Agastya voice plead with the Maruts to forgive and reconcile with Indra; RV 1.172 is a related short hymn.

### Questions

- Do not treat the reconstructed ritual story as a historical event.

<a id="mitra"></a>
## Mitra

Type: deity. Direct links: 1. Context links: 3.

### Direct Agastya links

- **C051** Agastya · Bhāgavata → mythic son of → Mitra. [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 6.18.5, 6.18.5](https://vedabase.io/en/library/sb/6/18/5/). translation_checked. The verse assigns shared Mitra–Varuṇa parentage. Mythic genealogy, not independently dated biological evidence.

### Context in the same passages

- **VEX008** Mitra → sees birth omen of → Vasiṣṭha. [The Rigveda: The Earliest Religious Poetry of India, Ṛgveda 7.33.10](https://wiswo.org/books/_resources/book-reference-pdfs/Jamison-Brereton-2014-The%20Rigveda-The%20Earliest%20Poetry%20of%20India%20all%203%20Volume%20Sets.pdf). translation_checked. The translation calls the lightning-radiance seen by Mitra and Varuṇa one of Vasiṣṭha’s births, and mentions another when Agastya brings him to the clan. Jamison–Brereton render this as one of two births; Griffith renders “one and only birth.” This claim follows the former without asserting historical biography.
- **VEX010** Vasiṣṭha → is described as maitravaruni → Mitra. [Ṛgveda 7.33, Ṛgveda 7.33.11](https://sacred-texts.com/hin/rigveda/rv07033.htm). translation_checked. Griffith translates Vasiṣṭha as the son of Varuṇa and Mitra. The verse belongs to a layered mythic account and does not establish historical parentage.
- **VEX013** Mitra → deposits seed in vessel with → Varuṇa. [Ṛgveda 7.33, Ṛgveda 7.33.13](https://sacred-texts.com/hin/rigveda/rv07033.htm). translation_checked. The hymn says the two gods poured their seed together into a vessel during a ritual gathering. The verse then names Māna as arising from the middle and says that the sage Vasiṣṭha was born from him; do not equate Māna with Agastya.

### Review notes

- RV 7.33.10–13 pairs Mitra with Varuṇa in Vasiṣṭha's birth imagery.

### Questions

- The hymn does not offer a historical chronology for divine or sage figures.

## Nacciṉārkkiṉiyar

Type: commentator. Direct links: 1. Context links: 1.

### Direct Agastya links

- **C059** Nacciṉārkkiṉiyar → writes about → Akattiyar · Tamil traditions. [Kamil Zvelebil, Pre-history of Tamil Literature, p. 15](https://www.tamiluniversity.ac.in/english/wp-content/uploads/2018/08/paper_01-PDF.pdf). scholarly_report. The commentator links Tolkāppiyar to Agastya.

### Context in the same passages

- **TEX_009** Nacciṉārkkiṉiyar → commentary narrates migration with → Vēḷir. [Iravatham Mahadevan, Meluhha and Agastya (2009), §4.11, pp. 15–16](https://www.harappa.com/sites/default/files/pdf/meluhha_and_agastya_2009.pdf). scholarly_report. Mahadevan reports that Nacciṉārkkiṉiyar’s Tolkāppiyam commentary has Akattiyar lead eighteen Vēḷir families, eighteen kings, and Aruvaḷar from Tuvarāpati south, with Potiyil as his eventual abode. This is a commentary narrative reported by a modern scholar. Tuvarāpati = Dvārakā is an identification, and the story supplies no verified migration date.

### Review notes

- Zvelebil reports that his Tolkāppiyam preface commentary names Tolkāppiyar as an Akattiyar pupil; Mahadevan reports a separate southern-migration narrative in the commentary.

### Questions

- Check the actual Tamil commentary text and distinguish its wording from later editorial summaries.

<a id="nahusha"></a>
## Nahuṣa

Type: person. Direct links: 2. Context links: 1.

### Direct Agastya links

- **C048** Agastya · Mahābhārata → curses → Nahuṣa. [Mahābhārata, Udyoga Parva, Ganguli §17, Udyoga §17](https://sacred-texts.com/hin/m05/m05017.htm). translation_checked. Agastya recounts cursing Nahuṣa to serpent existence. Ganguli gives ten thousand years for the curse; this is not Agastya’s age.
- **EEX020** Nahuṣa → touches with foot → Agastya · Mahābhārata. [Mahābhārata, Udyoga Parva, Ganguli §17, Udyoga Parva, Ganguli §17](https://sacred-texts.com/hin/m05/m05017.htm). translation_checked. In Agastya’s account to Indra, Nahuṣa touches the sage’s head with his foot while the sages carry him; Agastya then curses him to fall from heaven and roam as a serpent for ten thousand years. This adds the trigger and sequence to the core curse claim. Ten thousand years describes Nahuṣa’s curse, not Agastya’s lifespan.

### Context in the same passages

- **RFX008** Nahuṣa → corresponds to puranic witness → Nahuṣa · Viṣṇu Purāṇa witness. [Sörensen, Index to the Names in the Mahābhārata, Nahuṣa 2, Nahuṣa 2, record 7485](https://github.com/sanskrit-lexicon/csl-orig/blob/main/v02/inm/inm.txt#L85413). scholarly_report. This is a cross-text identification based on a secondary concordance; both nodes and their source-specific claims remain visible.

### Review notes

- Udyoga Parva §17 supplies the kick as the trigger of Agastya’s curse and gives Nahuṣa’s serpent-term; it is not an Agastya lifespan.

Type: commentator. Direct links: 2. Context links: 1.

### Direct Agastya links

- **C060** Pērāciriyar → writes about → Akattiyar · Tamil traditions. [Kamil Zvelebil, Pre-history of Tamil Literature, pp. 10, 15](https://www.tamiluniversity.ac.in/english/wp-content/uploads/2018/08/paper_01-PDF.pdf). scholarly_report. Pērāciriyar defends the pupil tradition.
- **TEX_004** Pērāciriyar → attributes threefold tamil division to → Akattiyar · Tamil traditions. [Kamil Zvelebil, Pre-history of Tamil Literature, pp. 10–11](https://www.tamiluniversity.ac.in/english/wp-content/uploads/2018/08/paper_01-PDF.pdf). scholarly_report. Zvelebil reports Pērāciriyar’s attribution to Akattiyan of Tamil’s three divisions: iyal, icai, and nāṭakam; he also describes Akattiyam as the foundational text for Tolkāppiyam. These are statements attributed to the commentary, not surviving contents of a complete Akattiyam.

### Context in the same passages

- **TEX_003** Pērāciriyar → defends traditional teacher relation → Tolkāppiyar. [Kamil Zvelebil, Pre-history of Tamil Literature, p. 15](https://www.tamiluniversity.ac.in/english/wp-content/uploads/2018/08/paper_01-PDF.pdf). scholarly_report. Pērāciriyar acknowledges a view that Tolkāppiyar followed other now-lost grammatical works, then argues that he was Akattiyar’s foremost pupil and followed his teaching. Reports a debate among commentators and scholars; it does not establish a historical teacher-pupil relationship.

### Review notes

- Zvelebil reports that he defended Akattiyar’s foundational role and Tolkāppiyar’s pupil status against an alternative account.

### Questions

- Verify the cited Poruḷatikāram commentary passages in a reliable Tamil edition.

- **TL039** Pīḷivaḷai · Maṇimēkalai witness → is daughter of → Vāsa Mayilai · Maṇimēkalai witness. [Maṇimēkalai · English translation by Kausalya Hart, Canto 24, lines 24-050–24-070 (Hart numbering)](https://www.projectmadurai.org/pm_etexts/utf8/pmuni0710.html). translation_checked. - **TL040** Pīḷivaḷai · Maṇimēkalai witness → is predicted to bear child of solar lineage prince → Prince of the Sun dynasty · predicted role in Maṇimēkalai. [Maṇimēkalai · English translation by Kausalya Hart, Canto 24, lines 24-050–24-070 (Hart numbering)](https://www.projectmadurai.org/pm_etexts/utf8/pmuni0710.html). translation_checked. An astrologer predicts Peelivalai will love a prince of the Sun dynasty and bear a boy; the passage does not name the child’s father. The Jain sage recounts an astrologer’s prediction. The text does not explicitly identify the predicted prince as Nedumudikkilli.
- **TL065** Pīḷivaḷai · Maṇimēkalai witness → gives child to → Kambala Chetti · merchant in Maṇimēkalai. Deepathilahai says Peelivalai gave her baby boy to the rug merchant Kambala Chetti and asked him to take the child with him. The child is unnamed; no independent claim about the boy’s father is added here.
- **TFNL023** Aṟavaṇa Aṭikaḷ · Maṇimēkalai witness → tells story of → Pīḷivaḷai · Maṇimēkalai witness. [Maṇimēkalai · English translation by Kausalya Hart, Canto 29, lines 29-001–29-030 (Hart numbering)](https://www.projectmadurai.org/pm_etexts/utf8/pmuni0710.html). translation_checked. Aravanar begins the story of Peelivalai and the lost child while teaching Maṇimekalai. The translation’s canto heading also names Killivalai/Nedungilli, but the primary verse begins with Killi; this batch does not assert that either matches the distinct Nedumudikkilli node from canto 25.
- **TFNL024** Pīḷivaḷai · Maṇimēkalai witness → gave birth to → Unnamed son of Peelivalai · Maṇimēkalai prior-birth story. [Maṇimēkalai · English translation by Kausalya Hart, Canto 29, lines 29-001–29-015 (Hart numbering)](https://www.projectmadurai.org/pm_etexts/utf8/pmuni0710.html). translation_checked. The story says Peelivalai bore a baby boy. Passage-level evidence from Hart’s English translation; this is a textual witness, not independent historical evidence.
- **TFNL025** Pīḷivaḷai · Maṇimēkalai witness → gave child to → Kambala Chetti · merchant in Maṇimēkalai. [Maṇimēkalai · English translation by Kausalya Hart, Canto 29, lines 29-005–29-015 (Hart numbering)](https://www.projectmadurai.org/pm_etexts/utf8/pmuni0710.html). translation_checked. Peelivalai gives her child to a carpet merchant, identified by Tamil name Kambala Chetti in the verse. Hart’s English renders the role as “carpet merchant”; the personal name Kambala Chetti is visible in the Tamil verse in this same canto. The child remains unnamed.

<a id="tolkappiyar"></a>
## Tolkāppiyar

Type: person. Direct links: 2. Context links: 1.

### Direct Agastya links

- **C061** Akattiyar · Tamil traditions → traditionally teaches → Tolkāppiyar. [Kamil Zvelebil, Pre-history of Tamil Literature, pp. 9, 15](https://www.tamiluniversity.ac.in/english/wp-content/uploads/2018/08/paper_01-PDF.pdf). scholarly_report. Tolkāppiyar is presented as Agastya’s pupil. A commentary tradition; not an explicit statement in the Tolkāppiyam base text.
- **TEX_002** Tolkāppiyar → commentarially identified as pupil of → Akattiyar · Tamil traditions. [Kamil Zvelebil, Pre-history of Tamil Literature, p. 15](https://www.tamiluniversity.ac.in/english/wp-content/uploads/2018/08/paper_01-PDF.pdf). scholarly_report. Nacciṉārkkiṉiyar’s commentary on the Tolkāppiyam preface identifies Tolkāppiyar as Tiraṇatūmākkiṉi, son of Camata(k)kiṉi, and a pupil of Akattiyar. The attribution belongs to the commentator’s account, not to an explicit statement in the Tolkāppiyam base text.

### Context in the same passages

- **TEX_003** Pērāciriyar → defends traditional teacher relation → Tolkāppiyar. [Kamil Zvelebil, Pre-history of Tamil Literature, p. 15](https://www.tamiluniversity.ac.in/english/wp-content/uploads/2018/08/paper_01-PDF.pdf). scholarly_report. Pērāciriyar acknowledges a view that Tolkāppiyar followed other now-lost grammatical works, then argues that he was Akattiyar’s foremost pupil and followed his teaching. Reports a debate among commentators and scholars; it does not establish a historical teacher-pupil relationship.

### Review notes

- A pupil relationship with Akattiyar is a commentarial tradition attributed particularly to Nacciṉārkkiṉiyar and defended by Pērāciriyar; Zvelebil says neither the Tolkāppiyam base text nor its prefatory stanza names Agastya.

### Questions

- Collate Nacciṉārkkiṉiyar’s and Pērāciriyar’s Tamil commentary passages directly against reliable editions and variants.

Tugra’s son is invoked as a precedent. Retain the wording Tugra’s son; do not automatically resolve to a unique Bhujyu.

### Review notes

- RV 1.180.5, in a hymn attributed to Agastya, recalls the Aśvins' rescue of Tugra's son.
- RV 1.117.15 also recalls the Aśvins rescuing Tugra’s son, separate from the Agastya verse at 1.117.11.

### Questions

- The wording does not itself securely identify Tugra's son with a particular named figure such as Bhujyu.
- Jamison–Brereton identify Tugra’s son with Bhujyu in their translation; this remains an editorial identification rather than an explicit name in 1.117.15.

<a id="velir"></a>
## Vēḷir

Type: people_collective. Direct links: 1. Context links: 2.

### Direct Agastya links

- **C065** Akattiyar · Tamil traditions → traditionally leads → Vēḷir. [Iravatham Mahadevan, Meluhha and Agastya (2009), §4.11, p. 16](https://www.harappa.com/sites/default/files/pdf/meluhha_and_agastya_2009.pdf). scholarly_report. The Vēḷir accompany the southern migration.

### Context in the same passages

- **TEX_008** Vēḷir → claims lineage from vessel of → Unnamed northern sage · Puṟanāṉūṟu 201. [Puṟanāṉūṟu 201 · literal translation excerpt in Mahadevan, Puṟam 201:8–12; Mahadevan §4.9, pp. 13–14](https://www.harappa.com/sites/default/files/pdf/meluhha_and_agastya_2009.pdf). scholarly_report. Kapilar’s poem praises a Vēḷ chief as descended through forty-nine generations from a lineage said to arise from an unnamed northern sage’s vessel and rule Tuvarai. Mahadevan paraphrases Puṟanāṉūṟu 201 and separately proposes identifying the unnamed sage as Agastya. The poem itself and its translation have not been independently checked here.
- **TEX_009** Nacciṉārkkiṉiyar → commentary narrates migration with → Vēḷir. [Iravatham Mahadevan, Meluhha and Agastya (2009), §4.11, pp. 15–16](https://www.harappa.com/sites/default/files/pdf/meluhha_and_agastya_2009.pdf). scholarly_report. Mahadevan reports that Nacciṉārkkiṉiyar’s Tolkāppiyam commentary has Akattiyar lead eighteen Vēḷir families, eighteen kings, and Aruvaḷar from Tuvarāpati south, with Potiyil as his eventual abode. This is a commentary narrative reported by a modern scholar. Tuvarāpati = Dvārakā is an identification, and the story supplies no verified migration date.

### Review notes

- Puṟanāṉūṟu 201’s translated passage ties a Vēḷ lineage to a northern sage’s vessel and forty-nine generations; Nacciṉārkkiṉiyar’s migration account is separately reported as leading Vēḷir groups south.

### Questions

- Check the Old Tamil poem and commentary directly; keep the poem’s unnamed sage separate from the named Agastya of the commentary tradition.

## Search log

A search log records checked leads. It is not a claim of exhaustive coverage.

### Vedic

- **Jamison Brereton Rigveda 1.165 1.170 1.171 Agastya Maruts translation commentary**: Inspected the accessible 2014 translation/commentary; it explicitly discusses the three-hymn sequence, its inferred story, and editorial voice assignments.
- **Rigveda 7.33.10–13 Mitra Varuna Urvasi Agastya Vasistha translation**: Inspected the metrical Sanskrit text at UT Austin and existing Griffith translation source record; verses 10–13 contain the birth imagery and named figures summarized above.
- **Rigveda Agastya Trasadasyu Purukutsa direct connection**: No direct relevant connection verified in inspected sources; left as an open question rather than adding claims.
- **Rigveda 1.117.11 Agastya Viśpalā Aśvins translation and Viśpalā referent**: Inspected Jamison–Brereton 2014 verse and translation; Agastya’s formulation is connected to the Aśvins restoring Viśpalā. Debate over the Viśpalā referent remains explicitly unresolved.

### Epic

- **Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa Aranya Kāṇḍa sargas 11–13 primary prose Agastya Sutīkṣṇa Rama Lakṣmaṇa Sītā**: Inspected narrative paragraphs at valmikiramayan.net; extracted visit sequence, audience request and weapons gift; excluded commentary paragraphs.
- **Mahābhārata Vana Parva Ganguli §§96–99 Agastya Lomasa Lopamudra Vātāpi Dridhasyu**: Inspected primary translation pages; added contextual family, narrative-sequence, and deed claims while preserving Ganguli numbering.
- **Mahābhārata Vana Parva Ganguli §§103–104 Agastya Vindhya south return**: Inspected primary translation; recorded the promised return and narrator’s present-tense non-return as internal narrative synchronism only.
- **Mahābhārata Udyoga Parva Ganguli §17 Agastya Nahusha Indra Salya**: Inspected primary translation; distinguished Agastya’s speech to Indra inside Śalya’s narration from direct contact with Yudhiṣṭhira.
- **Bhāgavata Purāṇa Agastya Indradyumna Śuka core graph audit**: No new primary passage claim; existing graph already contains the checked Bhāgavata claims. Kept this Indradyumna source-local.

### Tamil

- **Project Madurai Maṇimēkalai Kausalya Hart Agastya**: Located and inspected Hart’s English translation, including canto 1, the prologue, and canto 22; named narrative references checked.
- **Tolkāppiyam Agastya Nacciṉārkkiṉiyar Pērāciriyar commentary**: Inspected Zvelebil’s discussion and the translated scholarly report; found explicit separation between base grammar and commentarial pupil tradition.

- **Cilappatikāram English Agastya primary translation**: Found CICT catalog information and Zvelebil’s report on text/commentary references, but no accessible translation passage was checked for a new claim.
- **Paripāṭal Agastya primary translation**: Secondary leads found only; no passage added because the underlying Tamil/translation was not checked.
- **Buddhist Akitti Agastya identity**: No identity claim added; the Akitti/Agastya comparison remains an unverified comparative lead outside the accepted claims in this file.
